title: Tax planning after your business crosses $1 million
description: A practical agenda for coordinating the business, the owner's income, and the next stage of growth.
intro: A million dollars in annual sales is a business milestone. It is not a million dollars of taxable profit, and it does not identify the right entity or tax strategy by itself. Start a planning conversation with the economics of the business: operating margin, cash available to the owner, payroll, capital spending, and the owner's other income.

sections.title: Start with the whole picture
sections.text: Create a single view of each entity, its owners, the latest financial statements, and the tax returns already filed. Add an estimate of the current year's results and a cash forecast. A useful plan should explain how a proposed decision affects both the company and the owner, and distinguish a timing benefit from a permanent change in tax cost.

sections.title: Ask for an implementation calendar
sections.text: A recommendation only becomes useful when someone owns the next step. Ask which decisions need a payroll change, which require documentation, which belong in the books, and which require an election or another filing. Set a review date and identify the professional responsible for confirming each requirement.

checklist: Current profit and loss statements and balance sheets for every entity
Prior business and personal returns, with depreciation schedules
Payroll totals, owner payments, loans, and distributions
Planned hiring, purchases, acquisitions, or a possible sale
questions: Which decisions materially change my after-tax cash position?
What assumptions would cause the recommendation to change?
Who will implement and monitor the plan?

title: Revenue, profit, and owner cash are three different numbers
description: Why a seven-figure company can still need a better cash and tax forecast.
intro: Revenue measures sales. Profit reflects the earnings after the expenses included in the relevant financial statement. Cash available to an owner also depends on collections, debt payments, purchases, working capital, and the timing of tax payments. These numbers can move in different directions in the same month.

sections.title: Build a bridge from profit to cash
sections.text: Review receivables, payables, debt principal, capital purchases, inventory, and changes in customer deposits alongside the profit and loss statement. Identify cash committed to payroll and other operating needs before considering an owner withdrawal. A growing business can require more working capital even while reported profit improves.

sections.title: Keep the tax forecast separate
sections.text: Book profit and taxable income can differ. Ask your adviser to identify the adjustments rather than assuming the amount in the accounting software is the amount on the return. A useful dashboard shows operating profit, expected taxable income, and cash available after reserves as separate lines.

checklist: Monthly profit and loss statement and balance sheet
Debt repayment and capital purchase schedule
Rolling cash forecast with an explicit tax reserve
questions: How much of this month's profit has actually been collected?
Which cash payments are not expenses on the income statement?
What amount is available to distribute after operating reserves?

title: When an established owner should review entity structure
description: Bring ownership, operating plans, and owner cash needs into the same conversation.
intro: The entity decision should follow the business, its owners, and its plans. An LLC label alone does not tell you how the business is taxed. A review should consider the legal structure, the federal and state tax treatment, administrative costs, eligibility requirements, and how the owner expects to use the cash.

sections.title: Define the decision before comparing entities
sections.text: Write down whether the business expects to reinvest earnings, distribute cash, bring in investors, add partners, or prepare for an exit. Include the states where the company operates and the owner's expected income from other sources. Ask for a comparison that uses the same operating assumptions for each alternative.

sections.title: Include the cost of changing
sections.text: A proposed entity change can affect payroll, books, contracts, ownership rights, and filings. Ask tax and legal advisers to coordinate the effective date, required steps, and potential consequences. The lowest headline rate is not a complete measure of the owner's result.

checklist: Formation documents and existing tax elections
Projected profit, reinvestment, and distribution needs
Expected investors, acquisitions, or an exit
questions: What is the total company-and-owner result under each option?
Which restrictions apply to the proposed tax treatment?
What does the transition require?

title: An owner compensation review that starts with the work
description: Separate wages, distributions, reimbursements, and loans before making changes.
intro: Owner payments need a clear purpose and consistent records. A salary, a distribution, a reimbursement, and a loan are not interchangeable labels. For an S corporation, the IRS requires reasonable compensation for shareholder services before non-wage distributions are used as a substitute for that compensation.

sections.title: Document responsibilities
sections.text: Describe the owner's duties, time spent, experience, management responsibilities, and the work performed by other employees. Bring payroll records and relevant compensation information to the review. A percentage-of-profit shortcut should not replace an analysis of the services actually provided.

sections.title: Reconcile what the books show
sections.text: Review the payroll ledger, owner distributions, expense reimbursements, and shareholder loan accounts together. Ask the adviser to identify amounts needing correction and explain how those corrections flow into the books and returns. Schedule another review when the owner's role changes materially.

checklist: Owner job description and time commitments
Payroll records and existing wage calculation
questions: What evidence supports the compensation amount?
Do the books distinguish each type of owner payment?
When should we reassess the owner's role?

title: A quarterly tax-planning agenda for growing owners
description: Make the conversation about current results and upcoming decisions.
intro: A quarterly review works best when it starts with updated numbers and ends with decisions, owners, and dates. Bring the year-to-date financial statements, a full-year forecast, payroll information, and a list of decisions likely to happen before the next meeting.

sections.title: Use a current forecast
sections.text: Compare actual results with the assumptions used at the previous meeting. Flag unusual receipts, a major contract, a planned asset purchase, a new location, or an acquisition. Ask the adviser to show how the changed forecast affects the tax-payment plan and the owner's cash needs.

sections.title: Record the decisions
sections.text: Keep a short action register identifying the task, the person responsible, the required documentation, and the target completion date. At the next review, check whether the work happened and whether the facts still support the decision. Separate recommendations from items already implemented.

checklist: Year-to-date financials and updated full-year forecast
Tax payments made and available confirmations
Open implementation items from the previous review
questions: What has changed since the last forecast?
Which decision needs attention before the next meeting?
What documents or approvals are still missing?

title: Build a tax reserve around a forecast, not a guess
description: Coordinate owner income, payment timing, and business cash needs.
intro: A flat percentage of revenue rarely captures an owner's full tax picture. Start with projected taxable income, withholding, payments already made, the entity's tax treatment, and the owner's other income. Ask the adviser to distinguish the estimated final liability from the payments needed during the year.

sections.title: Create a payment map
sections.text: List each payment obligation, the taxpayer making the payment, and the relevant payment channel. Keep evidence of payments where the tax team can find it. The business's payment obligations and the owner's personal obligations should be identified separately.

sections.title: Refresh the forecast when results change
sections.text: A large new contract, weaker margins, an owner distribution, or a major transaction can change the assumptions. Agree on a trigger for revisiting the reserve, rather than waiting until filing time. Keep the operating cash forecast visible so tax payments do not collide with payroll or other commitments.

checklist: A calendar identifying taxpayer, amount, and review date
questions: Does the reserve reflect profit rather than sales?
Which payment rules apply to each taxpayer?
What event should trigger a new forecast?

title: Make your books useful before asking for a tax strategy
description: A clean handoff reduces avoidable back-and-forth.
intro: Tax planning depends on numbers that the owner and adviser can understand. A reconciled balance sheet is as important as an income statement. Organize transactions so the team can tell what happened, who was paid, what the business acquired, and whether an amount belongs to an owner account.

sections.title: Close the month consistently
sections.text: Reconcile bank and credit-card accounts, review receivables and payables, and identify unresolved transactions. Add schedules for loans, fixed assets, payroll, and owner activity. Record questions as they arise rather than allowing them to accumulate until a filing deadline.

sections.title: Create a repeatable handoff
sections.text: Use the same folder structure and naming convention for each reporting period. Include a short explanation of unusual activity and a list of missing documents. Ask the tax team what additional schedules are needed for the specific business rather than assuming every company needs the same packet.

checklist: Profit and loss statement and balance sheet
Loan, fixed-asset, payroll, and owner schedules
Supporting invoices and a list of unresolved items
questions: Which balance-sheet accounts are not reconciled?
Who owns the remaining cleanup?
What information is missing from the tax handoff?

title: Build an expense reimbursement process owners can follow
description: Give business expenses a consistent path from receipt to books.
intro: A reimbursement process should tell the person submitting an expense what to provide, where to submit it, and who reviews it. Ask your tax adviser which reimbursement rules apply to the business and the person receiving the payment before adopting a policy.

sections.title: Make the business purpose visible
sections.text: Retain the receipt, identify the business purpose, and record the relevant date and participants when appropriate. Keep business and personal amounts separate. A bank or card statement may show a payment without explaining its purpose or providing all the supporting detail.

sections.title: Connect the policy to the books
sections.text: Assign responsibility for reviewing claims and recording approved payments. Reconcile advances and reimbursements so amounts are not duplicated or left in an unexplained account. Ask the adviser to confirm the policy's substantiation and timing requirements for the actual arrangement.

checklist: Clear treatment of advances and personal portions
A reconciliation between claims, payments, and the ledger
questions: Which reimbursement arrangement applies here?
What evidence and timing are required?
Who checks that the expense is recorded only once?

title: Plan the equipment purchase before choosing its tax treatment
description: Keep operational need, financing, and tax timing in one model.
intro: An equipment purchase is first an operating and cash decision. List the asset's purpose, expected use, financing terms, delivery schedule, and the date it will be ready for business use. Ask the adviser to evaluate the applicable tax treatment with those facts rather than assuming a purchase automatically creates a particular deduction.

sections.title: Compare the full cash cost
sections.text: Include down payments, debt service, maintenance, training, installation, and any working-capital effect. Separate the cash forecast from the expense recognized in the books and the deduction expected on the return. The three schedules may have different timing.

sections.title: Maintain the asset record
sections.text: Keep purchase agreements, invoices, financing documents, and information about business use. Ask which elections, classifications, and placed-in-service records the tax team needs. Discuss the potential effect of later sale or disposal before treating the initial deduction as the whole outcome.

checklist: Asset description, invoice, and financing terms
Expected operating benefit and total cash cost
questions: When will the asset be placed in service?
Which treatments are available under the actual facts?
What happens if the asset is sold later?

title: Prepare for a retirement-plan design conversation
description: Start with the owner, the workforce, and the company's cash commitments.
intro: Retirement-plan design is a company decision that includes employees as well as owners. Prepare workforce information, compensation records, existing plan documents, and a realistic view of the business's ability to fund contributions. A contribution goal by itself is not a plan design.

sections.title: Bring the workforce facts
sections.text: Ask the plan professional which employee information is required for eligibility and design analysis. Include expected hiring, compensation changes, and any related businesses. Coordinate the discussion among the tax adviser, plan administrator, and investment professional so assumptions are shared.

sections.title: Ask about ongoing obligations
sections.text: Understand administration, testing, funding, reporting, and employee communication before choosing a plan. Ask for an annual calendar and a named person responsible for each task. Model a weaker-profit year as well as the current year so recurring commitments are visible.

checklist: Employee census prepared for the plan professional
Contribution budget and an ongoing administration calendar
questions: How does the design affect eligible employees?
What costs and annual obligations accompany it?
Can the business support the commitments in a lower-profit year?

title: Tax questions to ask before buying another business
description: Organize the diligence conversation before signing the transaction documents.
intro: Before buying a business, define what is being purchased and which advisers are responsible for the tax, legal, and financial review. The headline purchase price does not explain the treatment of assets, liabilities, owner interests, or future payments.

sections.title: Reconcile the operating story
sections.text: Compare financial statements, tax returns, bank activity, payroll, and the seller's supporting schedules. Identify adjustments that are proposed rather than proven. Ask who will investigate discrepancies and what information must be resolved before a decision.

sections.title: Model the transaction structure
sections.text: Ask the transaction team to compare the proposed structure, allocation, financing, contingent payments, and expected post-closing cash flow. Include integration costs and the buyer's ability to operate the business after closing. Keep the purchase documents and the tax model consistent.

checklist: Proposed transaction structure and purchase agreement
Financial statements, returns, and supporting schedules
Asset, debt, payroll, and ownership records
Financing terms and post-closing cash forecast
questions: What exactly are we buying?
Which tax assumptions depend on the final agreement?
What obligations might remain after closing?

title: A year-end planning checklist for established owners
description: Bring the decisions forward while there is still time to act.
intro: A useful year-end review distinguishes decisions still available from work that is already complete. Start with an updated forecast and a list of changes in the business, the owner's circumstances, and planned transactions. Ask the adviser to identify the actual deadlines that apply to each item.

sections.title: Focus on decisions, not a generic deduction list
sections.text: Review owner compensation, capital spending, expense documentation, tax payments, benefits, and pending transactions. Ask why each recommendation fits the specific business and what records are required. Avoid purchasing something solely because it appears on a year-end checklist.

sections.title: Prepare the filing handoff
sections.text: Assign responsibility for final financial statements, payroll reporting, asset schedules, and missing documents. Keep a record of elections and decisions so the filing team can connect the plan to the return. Schedule an early follow-up for unresolved items.

checklist: Planned purchases, transactions, and owner payments
Benefits and payroll items needing review
A document and implementation list with named owners
questions: Which decisions have a deadline before year-end?
What has actually been implemented?
What does the filing team still need?

title: One-time tax planning or an annual retainer?
description: Compare a defined planning project with an ongoing advisory relationship using deliverables, decision frequency, implementation and total cost.
intro: Start with the decisions your business must make, then choose the service period. A one-time engagement and an annual retainer can both be useful. Neither label tells you how many entities are covered, who prepares returns, or whether anyone implements the recommendations. Ask each firm to price the same work before comparing the fee.

sections.title: When a defined project is a reasonable starting point
sections.text: A discrete decision can have a clear endpoint: reviewing an upcoming acquisition, organizing the tax implications of a new property, or mapping an entity change for further professional review. Define the question, the inputs, the written output and the deadline. The proposal should state what happens if the facts change before implementation and whether follow-up questions are included. A written plan alone does not establish that an election was filed or a payroll change was completed.

sections.title: When an ongoing relationship can help
sections.text: Recurring decisions create a different workload. A growing employer may need regular coordination among its bookkeeper, payroll provider and preparer. Ask for the actual meeting cadence, forecast updates and response process rather than assuming unlimited access. Confirm whether the retainer includes bookkeeping or preparation, or only advice based on records supplied by others. Identify the person who will notice when the forecast becomes stale.

sections.title: Build a comparable first-year and next-year total
sections.text: Put setup, historical cleanup, planning, implementation, returns and recurring support on separate lines. For an annual service, obtain the minimum commitment and renewal terms. For a project, identify extra charges for additional entities, changed transactions or another tax year. A smaller first invoice may leave major work outside scope. Compare the complete assignment, then consider the time you will spend coordinating it.

sections.title: A fictional decision to test the proposals
sections.text: A business owner has reliable bookkeeping and preparation but plans to buy a second operation in six months. One proposal offers a transaction review with a written deliverable; another offers quarterly planning and the review. Ask whether the quarterly work answers additional decisions the owner actually expects. If both proposals require separate legal and valuation work, include those dependencies in the calendar. This example illustrates a procurement choice, not a tax recommendation or a reported client result.

comparison.caption: One-time tax planning or an annual retainer?
rows: A named deliverable and defined support period
A recurring schedule and renewal boundary
Price the rework or new assignment
Define which forecast updates are included
Do not assume ongoing advice includes filing
Full project plus required additional work
Full committed period plus excluded work

checklist: A list of decisions and their expected dates
Current providers and the work they already perform
A line-item scope for each entity and tax year
questions: What tangible work will I have at the end of the paid period?
Who implements each recommendation and how is completion confirmed?
What changes would require another fee or engagement?

title: Bookkeeper or tax advisor: define the missing work
description: Separate recordkeeping, tax preparation and planning before hiring. Compare the outputs and handoffs your business actually needs.
intro: If the books are late, a planning meeting may not solve the immediate problem. If the books are accurate but a major decision is approaching, another set of monthly reports may not answer it. Describe the missing output before choosing a job title. Firms can provide several services, so compare the written scope rather than assuming every bookkeeper or advisor works the same way.

sections.title: Start with the condition of the records
sections.text: Ask when the last month was closed and whether bank, credit-card, loan and payroll balances were reconciled. Recordkeeping work can include categorization, reconciliation and financial reports, but the exact responsibilities vary. Specify who gathers receipts, reviews uncertain transactions and approves changes. A tax advisor using the books still needs to know which balances are reliable and which are provisional.

sections.title: Separate preparation from decisions made before filing
sections.text: Preparation turns records into a return for a particular tax year. Planning considers decisions and their possible consequences before or alongside that process. The same professional may do both under one agreement, or each may be separately priced. Do not interpret a return-preparation fee as an unlimited commitment to model acquisitions, compensation or ownership changes.

sections.title: Use one handoff instead of competing versions of the books
sections.text: Agree on the accounting system, the date through which records are complete and who can post adjustments. The preparer should receive the final trial balance and relevant supporting schedules. If an advisor proposes a change, the bookkeeper needs a documented instruction that the responsible professional has approved. Keep a record of which version informed the advice.

sections.title: Choose the first hire from the bottleneck
sections.text: For a fictional owner with three unreconciled months and an unanswered acquisition question, two tasks exist. The records must become usable, and the acquisition needs timely specialist review. Ask whether cleanup can finish before the decision deadline and which assumptions the advisor can work with meanwhile. Do not replace missing facts with an advertised savings percentage. This is a workflow example, not evidence that a particular provider is suitable.

comparison.caption: Bookkeeper or tax advisor: define the missing work
rows: A written decision analysis and action list
Review dates tied to decisions and new facts
Reliable financial inputs and clear assumptions

checklist: Date of the latest completed close
A list of software access and approval owners
questions: Which missing output will your service deliver?
Who approves and posts tax-related accounting adjustments?
What work stays with my current preparer or another specialist?

title: Switching tax advisors without losing the filing handoff
description: Plan a provider transition around open returns, records, payroll and access. Use a written handoff before ending the old engagement.
intro: A provider change creates two separate jobs: choosing the next firm and closing the old assignment. Before moving records or cancelling access, identify every open return, notice and promised deliverable. A new proposal does not automatically transfer responsibility for unfinished work. Confirm the transition dates directly with both teams.

sections.title: Make an open-work register
sections.text: List each entity and tax year, the filing or deliverable, current status, responsible professional and next agreed action. Distinguish a draft from a filed return and ask what evidence confirms filing. Record any extensions or payment tasks the providers say remain outstanding. A transition checklist is not a substitute for verifying a particular legal deadline.

sections.title: Request usable records rather than a single document dump
sections.text: Ask what the incoming firm needs: final returns, depreciation schedules, relevant elections, work supporting carryforwards, and current financial reports may serve different purposes. Obtain software exports in formats the receiving team can use. Do not assume a PDF of the return includes all underlying records. The availability and release of records depend on the engagement and applicable requirements; settle that directly rather than guessing.

sections.title: Control access deliberately
sections.text: Use the agreed secure intake channel for returns and identity information. Keep an inventory of delegated access to bookkeeping, payroll and tax portals. Grant only the access needed for the new assignment and agree when the outgoing team can finish its work. Avoid cancelling a system merely because a new advisor has been hired; ask who needs the records and for how long.

sections.title: Finish with a written responsibility confirmation
sections.text: Send both teams the proposed division of work and ask them to confirm or correct it. For a fictional business moving firms in the middle of a payroll quarter, the key question is who owns each remaining payroll and annual reporting task. A completed handoff names the responsible provider, the period covered and how the owner will receive confirmation. It does not simply say that the new firm has everything.

comparison.caption: Switching tax advisors without losing the filing handoff
rows: Do not confuse this with acceptance of old unfinished work
Usable exports with a recipient confirmation
A download link alone does not confirm completeness
Keep necessary access until assigned tasks are finished
Named owner for every open item
Document unresolved items rather than assuming transfer

checklist: Open-item register by entity and tax year
Requested-record list from the incoming firm
questions: Which open filings or notices have you explicitly accepted?
Which records are still missing or unusable?
Who confirms completion of each task after the handoff?

title: Local or online tax advisor: compare how the work gets done
description: Evaluate in-person and remote advisory options by relevant experience, state coverage, secure workflow and implementation responsibility.
intro: A nearby office can make meetings convenient. A remote team can make it easier to consider specialists outside your immediate area. Neither location nor delivery format establishes the quality of a tax analysis. Compare the professional assigned to your facts, the service boundaries and the way work moves from records to decisions.

sections.title: Match experience to the assignment
sections.text: Describe your actual entities, industry, states and upcoming transactions. Ask for the kinds of work the proposed team regularly handles without requesting confidential client details. The IRS explains that preparers have different skills and qualifications and provides tools for checking credentials. Verify the assigned person rather than relying only on a firm name or a directory label.

sections.title: Check state and specialist coverage
sections.text: An office in your city does not automatically cover every state where your business operates. A national website does not prove that a team handles your specific state issues either. List the relevant jurisdictions and ask who will address each one. If legal, valuation, benefits or other specialist work is needed, identify the referral or coordination arrangement and any separate fee.

sections.title: Walk through a real handoff
sections.text: Ask each candidate how you would submit a financial statement, resolve a question, review a recommendation and confirm an agreed action. Remote delivery needs clear secure upload and communication practices. In-person delivery still needs document tracking and written outcomes. Clarify response expectations and what happens when your usual contact is absent.

sections.title: Use the same example for both candidates
sections.text: For a fictional owner operating in two states and evaluating a property purchase, ask both firms to describe the inputs, decision meeting and implementation handoff. One may propose office visits and another video meetings. Compare who reviews the work, which deadlines are accepted and which outputs you receive. Choose the working arrangement you can maintain, not a presumed advantage from the meeting format alone.

comparison.caption: Local or online tax advisor: compare how the work gets done
rows: Confirm office availability and travel expectations
Confirm video, telephone and written follow-up practices
Agree on scanning and secure delivery
Agree on portal access and accepted file formats
Verify the assigned professional and jurisdictions
Verify the assigned professional and jurisdictions
Identify backup coverage and response expectations

questions: Who handles the issues in each state relevant to my business?
How do I review and retain the written recommendations?
What is the escalation process when a deadline is approaching?

title: A directory profile is a starting point, not a credential check
description: Use business and tax directories to discover candidates, then check the assigned professional, credentials, service scope and source dates.
intro: A profile can help you find a person or firm, but it may combine historical records, public descriptions and promotional information. Read what the listing actually establishes before relying on it. A founding relationship does not establish current ownership; a tax-services description does not verify a professional license or prove suitability for your assignment.

sections.title: Identify the claim and its source
sections.text: Record the exact claim you want to verify: business founder, current executive, credential holder or provider of a particular service. These are different questions. Follow the source linked for that claim and note its date. A company history may support a founding relationship without confirming the person’s current role. If a page provides no source for a material claim, treat it as unresolved.

sections.title: Check the person who will do the work
sections.text: The IRS points taxpayers to its directory of preparers with credentials and selected qualifications. Use it as one verification resource and understand what the result represents. Ask the firm which professional will prepare, review or advise on your assignment. Check the applicable professional regulator when license status matters. Do not assume every employee shares the credentials shown beside the founder’s name.

sections.title: Separate commercial relationships from evidence
sections.text: Business Owner Index is owned and published by AE Tax Advisors. A directory listing does not establish that a founder is an AE client or endorses AE. The publisher’s commercial relationship should be visible when evaluating recommendations. Use the directory to discover sources and questions, then obtain current service information directly from the provider.

sections.title: Keep a short verification record
sections.text: For a fictional candidate, write down the firm name, assigned individual, source URL, observation date, credential result and unresolved questions. Ask for a written proposal addressing your actual entities and decisions. If two sources disagree about a current role, do not silently choose the more favorable version; request clarification. The goal is a usable shortlist with known limits, not a badge that implies a full professional investigation.

comparison.caption: A directory profile is a starting point, not a credential check
rows: What it does not independently confirm
The person and qualification actually returned
Current suitability for your particular assignment
Outcomes not guaranteed by the agreement
Client relationship, endorsement or verified results

checklist: Exact name of the assigned professional
Source URLs and dates for material claims
Credential or regulator lookup appropriate to the claim
Written service proposal and unresolved questions
questions: Who will actually prepare, review and advise on my work?
Which claims in the listing have current supporting sources?
What information should be corrected before I rely on this profile?

title: Reconcile merchant payouts before using sales figures for tax planning
description: A practical bridge from processor sales to bank deposits, with fees, refunds, reserves and timing differences shown separately.
intro: A payment processor can deposit less cash than the sales report shows without either number being wrong. Fees, refunds, chargebacks, reserves and settlement timing can all sit between the sale and the bank. Before an owner uses a dashboard number to forecast profit or taxes, the bookkeeping team should explain that bridge. This guide is a reconciliation worksheet, not a rule that every item has the same tax treatment.

sections.title: Choose one period and one processor
sections.text: Download the detailed sales activity, payout report and bank transactions for the same period. Keep the report date, time zone, currency and account identifier with each file. Identify payouts that combine sales from several days or cross month-end. A useful reconciliation has an opening unsettled balance, current activity, cash received and a closing unsettled balance. Comparing a calendar-month sales total with deposits received that month can leave a timing difference that needs explanation.

sections.title: Separate deductions from the payout
sections.text: Give processor fees, customer refunds, disputes, reserve movements and other adjustments their own lines. Avoid recording a net deposit as both sales and a separate unexplained clearing entry. The team should be able to follow an individual sale into the processor report and then into a payout. If a refund refers to a prior period, retain that reference instead of moving it merely to make the current month balance.

sections.title: Resolve the exception list
sections.text: For a fictional shop, a processor reports $10,000 of activity, subtracts $300 of fees and sends $9,700 to the bank. That arithmetic explains the cash movement; it does not alone establish taxable revenue or deductible expenses. If the bank receives $9,200 instead, identify the additional $500 with records rather than labeling it miscellaneous. Assign each unresolved difference an owner, source document and review date.

sections.title: Deliver a repeatable close file
sections.text: Save the reports, reconciliation and approved adjustments together. Tell the preparer which accounting method the books use and identify any change from prior periods. IRS recordkeeping guidance calls for supporting records behind business transactions; a processor dashboard screenshot may not contain enough detail. Ask the accountant how the reconciled sales, fees and timing items should appear in the ledger and tax workpapers.

checklist: Processor sales and payout exports for the selected dates
Matching bank statement and transaction references
Fee, refund, dispute and reserve detail
An assigned list of unresolved differences
questions: Can each payout be traced to its underlying activity?
Which differences are timing items and which require correction?
Who approves the final sales and fee mapping?

title: Separate loan principal, interest and fees in your business records
description: Build a lender-to-ledger payment schedule instead of treating every loan payment as the same kind of expense.
intro: A business loan payment is a cash outflow, but its components may belong in different places in the records. The lender might apply money to principal, interest, fees or an escrow balance. A bank-feed description rarely explains the allocation. Prepare a payment schedule that your bookkeeper and tax preparer can reconcile before using debt service in a profit or cash forecast.

sections.title: Begin with the signed debt documents
sections.text: Collect the note, amortization schedule, lender statements and closing documents. Record the borrower, account number, original proceeds, payment frequency and any amendments. Keep guarantees and ownership information in the appropriate secure file. If proceeds went directly to a seller or paid off another lender, show that flow explicitly so the absence of a deposit is not mistaken for missing financing.

sections.title: Reconcile the lender balance
sections.text: For each payment, list the payment date, cash amount and the lender’s allocation. Compare the ending principal balance with the statement, and explain differences from the original amortization schedule. Variable interest, late payments, extra principal and modifications can change the result. Do not force a payment into an old schedule when the lender’s actual application differs.

sections.title: Keep cash forecasting separate from expense classification
sections.text: For a fictional payment of $2,000, a lender might apply $1,600 to principal and $400 to interest. The owner needs the full $2,000 in the cash forecast, while the accountant separately determines the ledger and tax treatment. Fees and financed costs require their own review. This example illustrates allocation only; it does not establish that any interest or fee is deductible.

sections.title: Prepare the year-end handoff
sections.text: Give the preparer beginning and ending balances, total payments, lender allocations, accrued items and any refinance documents. Flag debt involving an owner or another related entity for specific review. Retain the evidence for why an entry was made, not just the final total. Ask who will reconcile the loan account each month and update the forecast when terms change.

checklist: Current lender statements and payment detail
Separate interest, fee and escrow lines
Documents for new borrowing, refinancing or payoff
questions: Does the ledger balance agree with the lender?
Which payment components need separate accounting review?
Has the cash forecast included the whole payment?

title: Prepare an asset disposal file before removing equipment from the books
description: Document a sale, trade-in, scrap or retirement so the asset register and tax schedules can be reviewed together.
intro: Equipment can leave a business through a sale, a trade-in, a donation, scrapping or a move to another use. Deleting it from an asset list does not explain what happened. Build a disposal file while the evidence is available. The preparer needs the asset’s history and the disposal facts to evaluate the accounting and tax consequences.

sections.title: Identify the exact asset
sections.text: Start with the register description, acquisition date, original invoice, serial number and location. Link the item to its depreciation schedule and any later improvements. If one invoice covered several assets, explain which portion is leaving the business. A vague entry such as old equipment makes it harder to match the physical item with the cost and deductions already recorded.

sections.title: Describe what actually happened
sections.text: Record the disposal date, recipient, proceeds and transaction costs. For a sale, retain the agreement and proof of payment. For a trade-in, preserve the entire new purchase agreement and trade allowance rather than only the net check. For scrapping, document the decision and available removal evidence. Do not invent a sale price for an item that was not sold.

sections.title: Carry the history into the review
sections.text: The IRS identifies acquisition, improvement, depreciation and disposal information as relevant asset records. Ask the preparer to reconcile the disposal with the books and tax schedule. The cash received is not automatically the gain, and the remaining book balance is not automatically the tax basis. Avoid estimating a deduction or recapture amount without the necessary history and professional review.

sections.title: Close the operational loop
sections.text: Tell the people responsible for insurance, maintenance, property records and the asset register that the item has left. For a fictional machine sold during an upgrade, the disposal file should remain linked to the old machine even if the replacement uses a similar description. Keep the old tax records through the applicable retention period; removing an operational listing is not permission to discard its history.

checklist: Original acquisition record and asset identifier
questions: Can the disposed item be matched to the tax schedule?
What facts distinguish a sale from a trade-in or retirement?
Who confirms the books and asset register were updated?

title: Turn a physical inventory count into an accounting review file
description: Plan count instructions, discrepancy review and a documented handoff without assuming every count difference has the same treatment.
intro: A physical count is useful only when the business can explain what was counted, when it was counted and how the result relates to its records. A list of quantities does not by itself establish cost, ownership or tax treatment. Prepare the count as an operational process and a separate accounting handoff, particularly when stock moves during the count.

sections.title: Define the count boundary
sections.text: Record locations, product identifiers, units of measure and the cutoff time. Decide how the team will identify damaged goods, consigned items, customer-owned materials and goods in transit. Keep these categories separate for review instead of silently including or excluding them. Give counters a consistent instruction for opened cartons, partial units and products with similar names.

sections.title: Control movement and recounts
sections.text: Assign a person to track receipts, shipments and transfers near the count. Preserve original count sheets and record who counted and who checked material differences. A recount should explain the correction rather than erase the first observation. If operations cannot pause, the accountant needs a movement log to bridge the physical observation to the reporting date.

sections.title: Investigate quantity and value separately
sections.text: A missing unit, a duplicate system entry and an outdated cost are different problems. Create an exception list with the item, recorded quantity, counted quantity, explanation and proposed adjustment. In a fictional warehouse, ten damaged units should not simply disappear into a generic shrinkage total before someone assesses what happened. Accounting and tax treatment require the applicable method and supporting facts.

sections.title: Hand over the full reconciliation
sections.text: Deliver the count instructions, signed results, movement log, exception approvals and cost report. Ask the preparer which additional records support purchases and inventory valuation. Retain the approved final file and the original evidence. The objective is a traceable reconciliation that another reviewer can understand, not an adjustment chosen solely to reach a desired profit figure.

checklist: Count date, cutoff time and locations
Product list and units of measure
Receipts, shipments and transfers near cutoff
questions: Which goods belong to the business at the reporting date?
Can the count be bridged to the inventory ledger?
Who approves quantity and cost adjustments?

title: Reconcile transfers between related businesses before year-end
description: Track the sender, recipient, purpose and matching entries for money moving between entities.
intro: An owner may move money between companies to cover payroll, fund a purchase or settle a shared bill. The fact that the same person controls both companies does not explain how the transfer should be recorded. A transfer log gives each entity’s accountant the same facts and makes mismatched balances easier to find.

sections.title: Identify both sides of the movement
sections.text: List the sending entity, receiving entity, bank accounts, date, amount and currency. Link the bank evidence on both sides. Avoid using a person’s shorthand company names when legal entities have similar names. If money passes through an owner’s account, show each step rather than presenting it as a direct entity-to-entity transfer.

sections.title: Document the stated purpose
sections.text: Keep the agreement, invoice, funding request or other contemporaneous explanation. Separate proposed loans, reimbursements, capital movements and payments for services for professional review. The label on a bank transfer does not settle its legal or tax character. Ask the advisors which documentation and approvals are needed for the actual arrangement, particularly when ownership differs between entities.

sections.title: Compare the ledgers together
sections.text: Build a schedule showing the sender’s entry and the recipient’s entry beside each transfer. Investigate missing dates, exchange differences, netting and transfers posted twice. For a fictional $8,000 movement, one company’s receivable and another company’s expense may indicate that the teams understood the transaction differently. Do not solve that mismatch by changing a label without agreeing on the underlying facts.

sections.title: Assign responsibility for closing differences
sections.text: Have one coordinator circulate the unresolved schedule to both bookkeeping teams. Record the agreed correction, approval and posting reference in each entity. Retain the original evidence and the reason for the final treatment. A clean combined total is insufficient if the separate entities’ records remain inconsistent or if an obligation is unsupported.

checklist: Legal names and ownership context of both entities
Bank evidence for sending and receiving accounts
questions: Do both entities describe the transaction consistently?
What documentation supports the proposed classification?
Who confirms both sides have posted the correction?

title: Track customer deposits without confusing bookings, cash and earned revenue
description: Create a deposit schedule that connects customer agreements, cash receipts, delivery and refunds.
intro: A business can receive money before it completes the promised work. The booking report, bank balance and revenue figure may therefore answer different questions. Maintain a customer deposit schedule that explains the commitment behind the cash. The proper accounting and tax treatment depends on the agreement, method and facts; this guide helps prepare those facts for review.

sections.title: Connect cash to the customer agreement
sections.text: Record the customer identifier, contract or order, receipt date, amount and payment reference. Keep the terms governing delivery, cancellation and refunds. Describe whether the payment reserves capacity, covers a milestone or pays for completed work. Do not rely on a generic deposit account name when different agreements impose different obligations.

sections.title: Track delivery and changes
sections.text: Update the schedule when goods ship, services occur, milestones are accepted or the order changes. Link the supporting invoice, completion record or credit memo. A rescheduled job should remain visible, especially when the cash was received in an earlier reporting period. Separate a customer refund from a transfer between the company’s own bank accounts.

sections.title: Reconcile the open commitments
sections.text: Begin with the prior schedule, add new receipts, identify amounts applied or refunded and explain the ending balance. For a fictional event company, deposits for next season and receipts for completed events should remain distinguishable even if the processor pays them together. Match the total to the ledger and keep a list of items awaiting customer or operations confirmation.

sections.title: Give the preparer the agreement and method
sections.text: Ask the accountant to review the schedule against the company’s reporting and tax methods. Do not assume cash receipt, invoicing or delivery alone controls every situation. Preserve the history of changes and communicate the approved treatment to the billing team. This prevents operational staff from resolving an accounting question by simply renaming a payment.

checklist: Receipt dates and bank or processor references
questions: What obligation remains for each open deposit?
Which events support applying or refunding the amount?
Does the approved treatment match the accounting method?

title: Build a contractor invoice review file that supports the business expense
description: Connect the engagement, work delivered, invoice approval and payment without treating an invoice as the whole record.
intro: A contractor invoice may state an amount due while saying little about the business purpose or work performed. A usable expense file connects the agreement, delivery, approval and payment. That file helps the owner understand spending and gives the bookkeeper and preparer evidence to review. It does not by itself decide worker status, information-reporting duties or deductibility.

sections.title: Match the invoice to the engagement
sections.text: Record the vendor’s legal identity, contract, project and agreed billing basis. Check whether the invoice is for a deposit, milestone, time period or completed assignment. Identify reimbursed costs and materials separately when they are described that way in the agreement. Do not silently replace the vendor name with an employee or owner name because someone else submitted the bill.

sections.title: Document the work and approval
sections.text: Ask the person responsible for the project to identify what was received and whether it matches the invoice. Useful evidence may include a dated deliverable, service report, approved hours or acceptance note. Keep sensitive customer information in its proper system and reference it securely. Approval should explain the business reason for the expense rather than merely show that someone clicked a payment button.

sections.title: Check payment and duplicates
sections.text: Link the approved invoice to the bank or payment-platform transaction. Review duplicate invoice numbers, partial payments, credits and expenses billed through another supplier. For a fictional design project billed in three milestones, the final invoice should not be recorded again as the full contract total if earlier milestones are already in the books. Resolve the difference with the vendor and preserve the correction.

sections.title: Route separate compliance questions
sections.text: Tell the preparer who provided the work, where the service occurred and how payment was made. Ask the appropriate professional to review classification and reporting questions rather than assuming all vendors receive the same treatment. Retain approved vendor information through a secure process. A complete expense file supports review; it is not a substitute for that review.

questions: Does this invoice match the work accepted?
Has any part already been billed or paid?
Which classification or reporting questions need separate review?

title: Review unpaid customer invoices before forecasting owner cash
description: Separate receivables aging, collection expectations and accounting questions in the planning conversation.
intro: A profitable month can leave little cash for the owner when customers have not paid. An accounts-receivable aging report helps explain the gap, but age alone does not establish whether an invoice is valid, collectible or eligible for a tax adjustment. Prepare a review that joins invoice facts with the collection history and reporting method.

sections.title: Validate the open balance
sections.text: Match each significant receivable to its invoice, customer agreement and delivery record. Check unapplied receipts, credit memos, duplicate invoices and payments sent to another account. Confirm the aging report’s date and whether it measures age from invoice date or due date. An apparently overdue amount may result from a posting error that needs correction rather than a collection decision.

sections.title: Separate disputes from delayed payments
sections.text: Record whether the customer disputes the work, awaits an internal approval, has promised a payment date or has stopped responding. Keep dated collection notes and supporting correspondence. Avoid turning an optimistic verbal promise into a forecast certainty. If an employee proposes a credit or settlement, identify who can approve it and retain the agreed terms.

sections.title: Build a realistic cash view
sections.text: For a fictional company with $40,000 of open invoices, split expected collections by timing and confidence instead of treating the entire balance as next month’s cash. Show the effect on payroll, debt service and planned owner withdrawals. This is a management forecast, not a change to the ledger. Keep forecast assumptions visible so the owner can update them when customers pay or plans change.

sections.title: Bring tax questions to the preparer
sections.text: Explain the accounting method and how each disputed or potentially uncollectible amount was originally recorded. Ask what evidence and approvals are required before any adjustment. Do not assume every old invoice produces a deduction or that a collection forecast determines taxable income. Save the reviewed aging, supporting records and final posting decisions together.

checklist: Invoices, delivery evidence and customer terms
Unapplied cash and credit memo review
questions: Which balances are accurate but unpaid?
How much cash is realistically expected and when?
What facts are needed before any accounting or tax adjustment?

title: Keep a year-end adjustment log that the next bookkeeper can follow
description: Record proposed, approved and posted journal changes with supporting documents and the effect on prior reports.
intro: Year-end work often produces journal entries after an owner has already used the books for decisions. Without a change log, one team may rely on an old report while another uses the adjusted version. A clear adjustment record shows what changed, why it changed and whether the posting has reached every relevant system.

sections.title: Give each proposed change an identity
sections.text: Assign a reference number, entity, period, preparer and description. Attach the calculation and supporting document. Separate a proposal awaiting approval from an entry that has been posted. A spreadsheet sent by email does not prove that the bookkeeping file now contains the change. Keep the original report version so the effect can be understood.

sections.title: Explain the accounts and rationale
sections.text: Show the debit and credit accounts, amount and purpose in language the reviewer can follow. Link the entry to the reconciliation or decision that produced it. If the entry reverses later, identify the reversal date and who will perform it. Do not use a general cleanup description for several unrelated corrections that require different evidence or approvals.

sections.title: Track approval and posting
sections.text: For a fictional business, a preparer may propose an adjustment to an asset balance after reviewing an invoice. The log should identify who approved the change, who posted it and which report confirms the new balance. If the tax workpaper differs from the financial books by design, record the distinction rather than forcing the two to agree without explanation.

sections.title: Distribute the final version
sections.text: Provide the final trial balance, updated financial statements and completed adjustment log to the people responsible for forecasting and next year’s opening balances. Identify any unresolved items and the agreed restrictions on later changes. Preserve access to the electronic records and supporting evidence. The next bookkeeper should not need to reconstruct the close from scattered messages.

checklist: Adjustment reference, entity and accounting period
Final report version and open issues
questions: Is this entry proposed, approved or posted?
Can a reviewer explain the change from its supporting file?
Who has received the final adjusted reports?

title: Build a business record retention map before deleting old files
description: Classify returns, asset history, employment records and ordinary support before applying a destruction schedule.
intro: An old folder is not automatically safe to delete. Record-retention periods depend on what a document supports and the circumstances of the return or transaction. Build a map of record categories before applying a general cleanup rule. The IRS also notes that non-tax requirements may require keeping records longer.

sections.title: Classify the record before choosing a date
sections.text: Separate filed returns, supporting income and expense documents, employment records, asset history and active contracts. Identify the entity and tax year for each category. Keep records tied to an open dispute, examination, claim or other hold outside the routine destruction process. A storage system organized only by upload date can hide documents that still support a current balance.

sections.title: Treat asset history as a continuing file
sections.text: An acquisition invoice or improvement record may support depreciation and a future disposal calculation years after the payment. Link that history to the asset rather than scattering it among annual expense folders. The IRS generally ties retention of property records to the limitation period for the disposal year. Ask the preparer how this applies to the business’s actual property and transaction history.

sections.title: Document the retention decision
sections.text: Assign a responsible reviewer to each record category and record the rule or professional instruction being applied. Do not turn a common three-year reference into a universal deletion policy: the IRS lists exceptions and separate employment-record rules. Also check lender, insurer, contractual and other applicable obligations. The goal is a defensible schedule that reflects the documents you actually hold.

sections.title: Test retrieval before archiving
sections.text: For a fictional company moving files to lower-cost storage, retrieve a sample invoice, return and asset record before removing the working copies. Preserve readable formats, permissions and the relationship between the record and its index. Log authorized deletions and pause the process when a hold arises. A backup that nobody can restore is not an effective recordkeeping plan.

checklist: Record categories with entity and year
Retrieval test and authorized deletion log
questions: What current or future calculation does this record support?
Does an exception or other obligation require longer retention?
Can the archived file actually be retrieved and read?

title: Preserve business records when changing accounting software
description: Plan exports, opening balances, audit history and access before ending the old software subscription.
intro: A software migration can preserve the headline balances while losing the detail needed to explain them. Before ending the old subscription, agree which records will move, which will remain archived and how the team will retrieve both. Electronic records still need to be complete, accurate and accessible; a successful login to the new system is only one part of the handoff.

sections.title: Inventory the old system
sections.text: List ledgers, customer and supplier records, bank reconciliations, attachments, payroll interfaces, asset schedules and relevant history. Identify integrations that hold information outside the accounting application. Record who controls each export and its format. If the new system cannot import a category, designate a readable archive instead of assuming the data is unnecessary.

sections.title: Choose and reconcile the cutover
sections.text: Set a cutoff date and decide who may post changes before and after it. Reconcile the final old-system trial balance with the new opening balances, including receivables, payables, loans and clearing accounts. Keep the detailed schedules behind those totals. Record any conversion adjustments separately from ordinary business transactions so the next reviewer can distinguish migration work from operations.

sections.title: Test a transaction end to end
sections.text: Use a sample sale, purchase and bank payment to test document retrieval and account mapping. For a fictional company, a customer balance of $5,000 in both systems is insufficient if the invoices behind it differ. Check aged items, unapplied cash and attachments. Ask the preparer whether the available archive will support later review of the periods kept in the old system.

sections.title: Retain access until the handoff is accepted
sections.text: Agree who signs off the migration and which exceptions must be resolved first. Preserve exports and credentials through an authorized secure process. Do not rely solely on an inactive subscription remaining available indefinitely. Record the archive location, responsible owner, retention review and retrieval instructions so staff turnover does not sever access to the business history.

checklist: Archive owner, access and retrieval test
questions: Which detail stays outside the new system?
Do opening balances reconcile to the old closing records?
Can a future reviewer retrieve the supporting documents?

title: Reconcile payroll reports, cash payments and the general ledger
description: Separate gross pay, deductions, employer costs and remittances before relying on the payroll expense total.
intro: A payroll service may withdraw several amounts on different dates for one pay run. The bank total, employee net pay and payroll expense are therefore not interchangeable. Prepare a reconciliation that joins the payroll register, funding transactions and ledger entries. Specific payroll filing or correction decisions belong with the responsible payroll and tax professionals.

sections.title: Define the payroll period and records
sections.text: Collect the register for each pay run, funding notices, relevant liability reports and bank activity. Record pay dates separately from the periods worked. Identify off-cycle checks, voids, reversals and manual payments. If payroll spans entities or departments, preserve that allocation. A report for one company should not be silently combined with another because both use the same service login.

sections.title: Build a gross-to-net bridge
sections.text: Show gross compensation, employee deductions and net payments in separate columns. Identify employer costs and payroll-service fees separately from employee withholdings. Match withdrawals to their purpose rather than posting all payroll-related cash to wages. Ask the payroll team to explain any funding amount that does not agree with the corresponding report.

sections.title: Review unpaid or duplicate items
sections.text: For a fictional pay run, a replaced payment can create a second bank movement while the underlying compensation remains unchanged. Link the void, replacement and clearance records. Review payroll liabilities and confirm what has been remitted or remains open. Do not clear an unexplained balance just because the payroll service’s dashboard shows the latest run completed.

sections.title: Agree on the final handoff
sections.text: Give the bookkeeper the approved mapping and adjustment references. Give the preparer the reconciled annual reports and a list of corrections or unresolved items. The IRS identifies employment records as a distinct recordkeeping category, so preserve the source detail under the applicable retention policy. Make someone responsible for confirming that payroll reports and the ledger remain aligned after corrections.

questions: Does each cash withdrawal have a documented purpose?
Have voids and replacements been counted correctly?
Who confirms the final payroll and ledger totals agree?

title: Gross margin versus markup: a pricing worksheet for owners
description: Use the correct denominator when comparing product prices, direct costs and the amount available for overhead.
intro: Gross margin and markup describe the same price-and-cost relationship from different directions. Confusing them can produce a price that misses the owner’s target. Write down the selling price and the cost being used, then calculate both measures explicitly. The worksheet is a management example; your accountant should confirm which costs belong in the reported gross-profit figure.

sections.title: Start with a clearly defined cost
sections.text: Choose one product or service and a consistent period. Identify the direct costs included in the analysis and explain any excluded labor, freight, payment fees or returns. A supplier’s unit invoice price may not be the complete delivered cost. Avoid comparing one product’s fully loaded cost with another’s purchase price. Keep the cost definition beside the calculation so a later reviewer can reproduce it.

sections.title: Use a different denominator for each measure
sections.text: For a fictional item sold for $100 with a defined cost of $60, gross profit is $40. Gross margin is $40 divided by the $100 selling price, or 40 percent. Markup is $40 divided by the $60 cost, or approximately 66.7 percent. A 40 percent markup on a $60 cost would instead produce an $84 price. These are arithmetic examples, not recommended prices.

sections.title: Translate a target into a testable price
sections.text: If the owner sets a target gross margin, the implied price is cost divided by one minus the target margin expressed as a decimal. Before using that result, test whether the cost assumption is complete and whether customers will pay the resulting price. Include discounting and expected returns. A mathematically correct target price is not evidence that the market will accept it.

sections.title: Compare the result with operating profit
sections.text: Gross profit must still cover the costs excluded from the definition. Prepare a separate view of overhead and operating expenses instead of treating gross margin as owner take-home cash. Review realized prices after discounts against the list-price model. Assign someone to update costs and note when supplier pricing, delivery charges or the product mix changes.

checklist: Gross profit, margin and markup calculations
Date and owner of the next update
questions: Which costs are included in the denominator?
Is the target expressed as margin or markup?
Does realized gross profit cover the remaining operating costs?

title: Build a break-even sales worksheet before expanding overhead
description: Connect fixed costs, variable costs and contribution margin without confusing accounting break-even with cash availability.
intro: A break-even model asks how much activity is needed to cover the costs included in the model. It is useful only when its cost definitions and sales mix are visible. Keep the calculation separate from the cash forecast, because debt payments, purchases, taxes and collection timing can create cash needs even when a simplified operating model breaks even.

sections.title: Classify the costs for this decision
sections.text: List costs that change with the activity being modeled and costs that remain fixed within the relevant range. Explain mixed costs instead of forcing them into one category without a basis. A staffing or facility step-change can make a cost fixed at one volume and higher at another. State the period, capacity limit and product mix before calculating a target.

sections.title: Calculate contribution and break-even
sections.text: In a fictional business with $20,000 of monthly fixed costs and a 40 percent contribution margin, break-even sales are $20,000 divided by 0.40, or $50,000. Contribution margin here means sales less the specified variable costs, divided by sales. This example excludes items not listed in the model. It is not a claim about the business’s tax liability or required bank balance.

sections.title: Test the assumptions that move the result
sections.text: Calculate a second case with lower realized pricing, higher variable costs or a different sales mix. If contribution falls to 32 percent while fixed costs stay $20,000, the same formula produces $62,500 of sales. Identify which assumption management can observe each week. Do not present a single break-even number without showing how sensitive it is to the inputs.

sections.title: Connect the model to implementation
sections.text: Compare required volume with actual capacity, sales history and expected collection dates. Identify any additional hiring, equipment or inventory that the volume would require. Build those cash movements into a separate forecast. Have the accountant reconcile the model’s categories with the financial statements so differences are understood rather than hidden.

checklist: Fixed-cost schedule for the selected period
Separate cash forecast for financing and timing
questions: Which costs change at the modeled volume?
How much does the result move if contribution declines?
Can the business deliver and collect the required sales?

title: Review cash runway with scenarios instead of one countdown
description: Calculate a simple runway indicator, then test collection timing, restricted cash and changing outflows.
intro: Cash runway is often presented as cash divided by monthly burn. That shortcut can be informative, but it is not a promise about how long a company can operate. Start with cash that is available for the modeled purpose and define burn consistently. Then use a dated forecast to test how receipts, obligations and management decisions change the result.

sections.title: Define available cash
sections.text: Reconcile the bank balances to the books and identify funds committed or restricted for another purpose. Separate an approved borrowing facility from cash already received. Confirm which entities hold the money and whether the forecast assumes transfers between them. Record the observation date so a cash figure from last month is not combined with this month’s spending estimate.

sections.title: Show the shortcut calculation
sections.text: A fictional company with $120,000 of available cash and a steady $15,000 monthly net cash outflow has a simple eight-month runway indicator. Net outflow means cash payments less cash receipts under the stated definition. The indicator assumes that both amounts remain stable. It does not account for a large future payment, collection delay or financing event unless those effects are included.

sections.title: Replace the constant assumption with dated scenarios
sections.text: Build monthly or weekly receipts and payments through the relevant horizon. Show a base case and a downside case using different collection or sales assumptions. Add known annual payments and planned purchases on their expected dates. Keep an uncommitted financing proposal outside the base cash balance unless management deliberately labels it as a separate scenario.

sections.title: Agree on review triggers
sections.text: Identify the observable changes that require an updated forecast, such as slower collections, a hiring decision or a significant contract change. Assign a reviewer and keep prior versions with their assumptions. The purpose is to support decisions while alternatives remain available, not to turn an uncertain forecast into a precise survival date.

checklist: Reconciled and available cash by entity
questions: Which cash is actually available for operations?
What breaks the steady-burn assumption?
When will management revisit the forecast?

title: Measure customer concentration before planning the next year
description: Review revenue, receivables and cash dependence separately when one customer represents a large share of the business.
intro: A customer can be important in several different ways: revenue, profit, receivables, referrals or future contracted work. One concentration percentage does not capture all of them. Prepare a short review that identifies the measure, period and customer grouping used. The result should clarify dependence and possible responses without pretending to predict whether a customer will leave.

sections.title: Choose the measure and group related accounts
sections.text: Start with a consistent revenue period and reconcile customer totals with the ledger. Decide how related customer entities or departments are grouped and document the rule. A single organization billed under several names can otherwise appear more diversified than it is. Keep credits and returns in the calculation instead of using only gross invoices.

sections.title: Calculate revenue and receivable shares separately
sections.text: If a fictional customer produces $180,000 of a company’s $600,000 annual revenue, its revenue share is 30 percent. That does not establish its share of gross profit or cash collected. Compare the customer’s unpaid balance with total receivables at the review date, and investigate whether its payment timing creates a different exposure than its sales share suggests.

sections.title: Read the operating context
sections.text: List contract dates, renewal steps, service obligations and capacity dedicated to the customer. Ask which employees, inventory or equipment are difficult to redeploy. Distinguish a documented customer commitment from a sales forecast. Avoid interpreting a long relationship as a guarantee of future orders or a large order as proof of a permanent revenue stream.

sections.title: Test a response without inventing a prediction
sections.text: Model a delay or partial reduction as a scenario and show its effect on collections, variable costs and fixed commitments. Identify practical monitoring and diversification actions with an owner and review date. Keep the exercise separate from the official forecast unless management approves a change. The goal is to understand consequences and choices, not assign an unsupported probability to customer loss.

checklist: Contracts, renewal dates and committed capacity
questions: Which measure best explains the dependence?
Do related accounts need to be grouped together?
What action would change if orders or payments slowed?

title: Test a price change against volume and contribution
description: Use a simple scenario to compare a proposed price with expected units, variable costs and customer response.
intro: A price increase does not automatically increase profit, and a discount does not automatically increase useful sales. Model both price and volume, using a stated cost definition. Then compare the calculation with evidence about customer behavior and delivery capacity. Treat the example as a decision worksheet rather than a recommended price or a forecast guarantee.

sections.title: Build the current case from actual results
sections.text: Record units delivered, realized selling prices after discounts and the variable costs included. Reconcile these figures with the relevant sales and cost reports. Separate one-time credits or unusual orders that distort the period. Explain whether the model covers one product, a service package or a mixed portfolio, because an average price can conceal a changing mix.

sections.title: Calculate a proposed case
sections.text: For a fictional product selling 1,000 units at $100 with $60 variable cost per unit, contribution is $40,000. A proposed $110 price with 900 units and the same unit cost produces $45,000 contribution. This calculation assumes no other changes and excludes fixed costs. It illustrates why units and contribution need to be modeled together.

sections.title: Stress-test the response
sections.text: Run alternatives for larger volume loss, higher servicing costs or additional discounts. Identify the evidence behind each assumption, such as actual renewal conversations or a bounded customer test. Do not treat an informal guess as a measured demand curve. Include the cost of communicating and administering the change if it is material to the decision.

sections.title: Define the decision and follow-up
sections.text: Record the proposed effective date, customers affected and approval owner. Decide which measures will be reviewed afterward: realized price, units, cancellations, gross profit and collection timing. Compare the actual result with the assumptions and preserve the difference. A decision can be well documented even when the market response remains uncertain.

questions: How many units can change before contribution declines?
Which costs or discounts might move with the price?
What evidence will show whether the change worked?

title: Separate project profitability from project cash flow
description: Compare the economic result of a job with its billing, collections and payment schedule before deciding what cash is available.
intro: A project can appear profitable while consuming cash, or generate an early cash surplus before the work is complete. Keep its profit analysis and cash schedule side by side. Use a consistent definition of project costs and identify remaining obligations. The difference between the two views is information to explain, not an error to hide.

sections.title: Define the project boundary
sections.text: Identify the contract, approved changes, deliverables and review date. Separate work completed from work still expected. Include labor, subcontractors, materials and other costs under a documented rule. Ask the accountant how the management model relates to revenue and expense recognition in the books. A project spreadsheet should not silently change the company’s accounting method.

sections.title: Show two calculations
sections.text: In a fictional completed job, a $50,000 fee less $35,000 of defined direct costs produces $15,000 of project contribution before other costs. If only $30,000 has been collected and $20,000 paid at the observation date, net cash received so far is $10,000. The remaining receivables and unpaid costs explain part of the difference. Neither figure alone is owner distributable cash.

sections.title: Estimate remaining work separately
sections.text: For an open project, maintain an estimate-to-complete with its assumptions and responsible reviewer. Distinguish approved scope from hoped-for change orders. Identify rework, retention, disputed invoices and commitments that have not reached the ledger. Update the forecast when facts change rather than carrying the original budget forward automatically.

sections.title: Use the review for a concrete decision
